items.prompt: What is a 'formal model' (or abstraction), as used in this unit?
choices: A simplified, precisely defined representation of a real situation that keeps only the properties relevant to the question being asked
Any diagram drawn to explain a system to a new hire
The full, complete set of every true fact about a real situation
A synonym for 'documentation'
items.explanation: A formal model deliberately keeps only what a specific question depends on and discards the rest -- it is not 'all the facts,' and it is not decoration, it is a tool built to make a specific question answerable.
items.reference:
🎯 keeps only what the question needs
🗑️ deliberately discards the rest

Why: A model that tried to keep everything true about a situation would be as hard to use as the messy reality it was meant to simplify.

items.prompt: The spreadsheet in L1's scenario had accurate 'needs' data for six months, yet nobody caught the dependency cycle. What does that show about raw facts versus a formal model?
choices: Having accurate facts isn't the same as having a structure that lets you mechanically check a property like 'does a cycle exist'
The facts must have been wrong, since a correct model would have been obvious
Spreadsheets can never store dependency information
The team simply didn't read the spreadsheet carefully enough
items.explanation: The raw facts were correct the whole time. What was missing was a structure -- a graph, with known cycle-detection algorithms -- that could mechanically answer the cycle question instead of relying on someone noticing it by eye.
items.reference:
🎯 keeps only what the question needs
🗑️ deliberately discards the rest

Why: A model that tried to keep everything true about a situation would be as hard to use as the messy reality it was meant to simplify.

items.prompt: Two engineers model the same 'services and their dependencies' facts, but for different questions -- one for deploy order, one for on-call paging priority. Should they necessarily end up with the same model?
choices: Not necessarily -- each model should keep only what its own question depends on, which can differ even for the same underlying facts
Yes, always -- one correct model exists per real-world situation
No -- models are arbitrary and have no relationship to the question being asked
Yes, because more detail in a model is always better regardless of the question
items.explanation: The same real system can justify different models depending on what each specific question needs -- deploy order needs dependency edges; paging priority needs different information (like current on-call ownership) that deploy order doesn't.
items.reference:
🎯 keeps only what the question needs
🗑️ deliberately discards the rest

Why: A model that tried to keep everything true about a situation would be as hard to use as the messy reality it was meant to simplify.

items.prompt: In L1's scenario, what actually changed between the spreadsheet missing the cycle for six months and the cycle being caught in one script run?
choices: The underlying facts stayed the same; the representation changed to a structure a known algorithm could check
The services themselves were reconfigured to remove the dependency
The spreadsheet had incorrect data that was later corrected
More engineers were added to review the spreadsheet by hand
items.explanation: The 'needs' facts never changed. What changed was formalizing them as a graph, which made a well-known cycle-detection algorithm directly applicable.
items.reference:
📋 spreadsheet: same facts, no checkable structure
🕸️ graph: same facts, structure + algorithm

Why: Formalizing doesn't add new facts -- it makes existing facts usable by tools built for that structure.

items.prompt: Why couldn't the team just 'read the spreadsheet more carefully' to catch the cycle, as a general strategy for larger systems?
choices: Manual tracing doesn't scale -- the number of dependency paths to check grows much faster than the number of services
Spreadsheets are technically incapable of storing dependency data
Careful reading always catches every cycle regardless of system size
The cycle only existed because of a typo, not a structural gap
items.explanation: As services and edges grow, the number of possible paths to trace by hand grows much faster, so manual checking becomes less reliable exactly as the stakes of missing a cycle go up.
items.reference:
📋 spreadsheet: same facts, no checkable structure
🕸️ graph: same facts, structure + algorithm

Why: Formalizing doesn't add new facts -- it makes existing facts usable by tools built for that structure.

items.prompt: In a dependency graph, what does a 'cycle' mean in practical terms?
choices: A loop where nothing in it can ever be the first one ready, since each member is blocked on another member of the same loop
Any two services that both call each other's APIs at runtime
A service that has no dependencies at all
A path that visits every node in the graph exactly once
items.explanation: A cycle in a dependency graph means every node in the loop is waiting on another node in the same loop -- there's no valid starting point among them.
items.reference:
🔁 cycle: a path that returns to a node already on it
🚫 nothing in the loop can go first

Why: This is exactly why L1's spreadsheet cycle (accounts → audit-log → billing → accounts) hung a deploy forever.

items.prompt: L1's cycle was 'accounts needs audit-log, audit-log needs billing, billing needs accounts.' How many services are involved in this cycle?
items.explanation: Three services form the loop: accounts, audit-log, and billing, each depending on the next until it wraps back to accounts.
items.reference:
🔁 cycle: a path that returns to a node already on it
🚫 nothing in the loop can go first

Why: This is exactly why L1's spreadsheet cycle (accounts → audit-log → billing → accounts) hung a deploy forever.

items.prompt: How does this unit's skill relate to `state-machines`?
choices: State machines are one specific formal structure; this unit is about the broader skill of choosing which formal structure a messy problem calls for
They're unrelated topics that happen to share the word 'state'
State machines are a prerequisite math topic needed before graphs can be understood
This unit replaces state machines as the only formal structure worth learning
items.explanation: State machines (named states + legal transitions) are one instance of a formal structure, useful for lifecycle/workflow problems specifically. This unit is about recognizing which structure -- graph, state machine, constraint set, or relation -- actually fits a given messy problem.
items.reference:
🧩 abstraction: the general skill of choosing a structure
🔀 state machines: one specific structure, for lifecycles

Why: Recognizing the right structure to reach for is the harder, more general skill; state machines are the well-known answer for one specific problem shape.

items.prompt: A messy problem is 'an order moves through placed, paid, shipped, delivered, and only some transitions between these are legal.' Which formal structure from this unit fits best?
choices: A state machine -- named states plus legal transitions
A graph of unrelated services
A flat list with no relationships at all
A spreadsheet with no formal structure
items.explanation: A lifecycle with named phases and rules about what can follow what is exactly the shape a state machine is built for.
items.reference:
🧩 abstraction: the general skill of choosing a structure
🔀 state machines: one specific structure, for lifecycles

Why: Recognizing the right structure to reach for is the harder, more general skill; state machines are the well-known answer for one specific problem shape.

Constraint set
Mathematical relation
items.explanation: Relationships between discrete things -- dependencies, links, connections -- are exactly what nodes and edges (a graph) are built to represent.

Why: Matching the real-world shape of the problem to the structure built for that shape is what makes known algorithms applicable.

choices: Constraint set
Graph
State machine
Mathematical relation
items.explanation: Problems about fitting things together under limits -- time, space, capacity -- are exactly what a constraint set (variables plus the rules they must jointly satisfy) is built for.

Named phases + rulesState machine

items.prompt: How does this unit build on `problem-decomposition`?
choices: Decomposition breaks a vague problem into concrete pieces; this unit is about choosing a formal shape for those pieces so reasoning about them stops being ad hoc
They are identical skills taught twice under different names
Decomposition is only relevant to soft-skill tracks and unrelated to formal modeling
This unit replaces decomposition as an unnecessary earlier step
items.explanation: Decomposition gets you concrete, attackable pieces. This unit goes further: once the pieces exist, choosing the right formal structure to represent them is what makes precise reasoning -- not just manageable chunks -- possible.
items.reference:
✂️ decomposition: vague problem → concrete pieces
🧩 abstraction: pieces → a formal, reasoned-about shape

Why: Breaking a problem apart doesn't automatically make each piece precise to reason about -- that's a separate step.

items.prompt: After decomposing 'make checkout faster' into network/server/database/client time, what would formal modeling (this unit's skill) add on top?
choices: A precise structure for whichever piece needs deeper reasoning -- e.g. modeling database query dependencies as a graph to find the real bottleneck path
Nothing -- decomposition alone is sufficient for every problem
A requirement to rewrite the decomposition as a state machine regardless of the pieces' actual shape
Formal modeling only applies before decomposition, never after
items.explanation: Decomposition identifies which piece(s) matter; formal modeling gives whichever piece needs precise reasoning (e.g. a chain of dependent queries) a structure that known techniques can operate on.
items.reference:
✂️ decomposition: vague problem → concrete pieces
🧩 abstraction: pieces → a formal, reasoned-about shape

Why: Breaking a problem apart doesn't automatically make each piece precise to reason about -- that's a separate step.

items.prompt: A deploy-order graph models each service with its full incident history, CPU load, and on-call owner, in addition to its dependency edges. Is this a good model for the deploy-order question?
choices: No -- it's over-abstracted; none of that extra data affects deploy order, and every extra field is one more thing that can go stale or be misread
Yes -- more information about a service is always better for any model of it
No -- it's under-abstracted, because it's missing dependency edges
Yes, but only if the extra fields are kept perfectly up to date
items.explanation: None of the extra fields change whether one service can start before another. Adding them doesn't help answer the deploy-order question -- it just adds surface area for the model to be wrong or misread.
items.reference:
➖ under-abstraction: missing what the question needs
➕ over-abstraction: extra detail the question doesn't need
✅ just right: exactly what the question depends on

Why: Both directions of error are shown on the same underlying services, judged against the same specific question.

items.prompt: A deploy-order model lists every service's name but records no dependency edges at all. Is this a good model for the deploy-order question?
choices: No -- it's under-abstracted; it discarded the exact property (dependency order) the question needs, so it can't answer it
Yes -- a flat list is always the safest, simplest starting model
No -- it's over-abstracted, because names alone are too much detail
Yes, as long as the names are spelled correctly
items.explanation: A flat list without edges silently answers a different, easier question ('what services exist') than the one actually asked ('what order is safe'). That's under-abstraction: discarding a property the question genuinely depends on.
items.reference:
➖ under-abstraction: missing what the question needs
➕ over-abstraction: extra detail the question doesn't need
✅ just right: exactly what the question depends on

Why: Both directions of error are shown on the same underlying services, judged against the same specific question.

items.prompt: For the deploy-order question specifically, what does L2 identify as the 'just right' model of the same services?
choices: Each service as a node, with one directed edge per 'needs' relationship -- nothing more, nothing less
Each service with its full deployment history plus dependency edges
Each service as a name only, with dependency notes kept in a separate document
A single shared boolean flag marking whether the whole system is 'ready'
items.explanation: The deploy-order question depends only on the 'needs' relationships -- nodes plus directed edges capture exactly that, with nothing extraneous and nothing missing.
items.reference:
➖ under-abstraction: missing what the question needs
➕ over-abstraction: extra detail the question doesn't need
✅ just right: exactly what the question depends on

Why: Both directions of error are shown on the same underlying services, judged against the same specific question.

items.prompt: In L2's workflow for choosing a formal structure, what comes right after 'identify what actually varies and what the question depends on'?
choices: Survey the real-world shape of the problem (relationships? phases? limited resources? a rule?)
Immediately write production code implementing the chosen structure
Skip straight to verifying against real cases
Discard the problem as too messy to formalize
items.explanation: The workflow surveys the problem's real-world shape next, before choosing a structure -- matching the shape to a structure is what step 3 (choosing) depends on.
items.reference:
1Identify what varies / matters
2Survey the real-world shape
3Choose simplest fitting structure
4Formalize
5Verify against known real cases

Why: Skipping ahead to a structure before understanding the problem's shape risks forcing the wrong one, as L3's tree-mismatch example shows.

items.prompt: Why does L2's workflow include a 'verify the model against a few real cases you already know the answer to' step, rather than trusting a newly built model immediately?
choices: Formalizing doesn't remove the need to check the model against reality -- it just moves where mistakes get caught, from unnoticed to caught before broad use
Verification is optional busywork with no real purpose
Because formal models are always correct once built, so this step exists only for documentation
Because the workflow requires exactly five steps regardless of usefulness
items.explanation: A model built from wrong or mistyped source facts will confidently give wrong answers. Checking it against known cases before trusting it on new ones is what catches that early.
items.reference:
1Identify what varies / matters
2Survey the real-world shape
3Choose simplest fitting structure
4Formalize
5Verify against known real cases

Why: Skipping ahead to a structure before understanding the problem's shape risks forcing the wrong one, as L3's tree-mismatch example shows.

choices: Constraint set -- variables (reviewer assignments) plus rules they must jointly satisfy
Graph -- reviewers and PRs as nodes with no other structure
State machine -- reviewers move through named review phases
Mathematical relation -- a single if-then rule
items.explanation: Fitting assignments together under limits (self-review forbidden, a 3-PR cap) is exactly the shape a constraint set is built to solve -- a solver can find a valid assignment or prove none exists.
items.reference:
RelationshipsGraph
Named phases + rulesState machine
Fit under limitsConstraint set
If X then YMathematical relation

Why: Matching the real-world shape to the structure built for it is what makes a known solving technique applicable instead of ad hoc trial and error.

items.prompt: A messy problem is 'a discount applies only if the cart total exceeds $50 AND the customer has an active membership.' Which structure fits best?
choices: Mathematical relation / rule set -- deriving a consequence from conditions that must jointly hold
Graph -- carts and memberships as nodes
State machine -- the cart moves through named phases
Constraint set -- fitting the discount under a resource limit
items.explanation: 'If these conditions hold, then this consequence follows' is exactly the shape a mathematical relation / rule set is built to express and check for consistency.
items.reference:
RelationshipsGraph
Named phases + rulesState machine
Fit under limitsConstraint set
If X then YMathematical relation

Why: Matching the real-world shape to the structure built for it is what makes a known solving technique applicable instead of ad hoc trial and error.

items.prompt: L2's Checkpoint describes onboarding steps where some steps require others to finish first, AND a couple of steps are mutually exclusive. Why does a graph alone fall short here?
choices: A graph naturally expresses 'requires,' but has no natural way to express 'must never both happen' -- that's a constraint a plain graph would silently drop
Graphs cannot represent ordering at all
Graphs can only have one node
A graph would work perfectly and no other structure is needed
items.explanation: A dependency graph captures 'requires' well via edges and topological order, but 'mutually exclusive' isn't a dependency edge -- a constraint set is needed to capture both facts together.
items.reference:
RelationshipsGraph
Named phases + rulesState machine
Fit under limitsConstraint set
If X then YMathematical relation

Why: Matching the real-world shape to the structure built for it is what makes a known solving technique applicable instead of ad hoc trial and error.

items.prompt: A team wants to model 'safe to deploy in parallel this week' versus 'safe to deploy in parallel ever,' for the same 14 services. Should these use the same model?
choices: No -- 'this week' depends on time-bound facts like in-flight migrations, while 'ever' depends only on stable structural dependency edges
Yes -- both questions are about the same services, so one model always suffices
No -- because parallel deploys are never actually safe regardless of dependencies
Yes, as long as the model is updated once a year
items.explanation: The two questions depend on different, mostly-independent facts -- mixing them into one model means either polluting the stable structure with fast-changing facts, or treating time-bound facts as permanent.
items.reference:
📅 'this week': time-bound facts (migrations, flags)
🏗️ 'ever': stable structural dependency edges

Why: The question being asked determines what belongs in the model -- not everything true about the underlying services.

items.prompt: What's the risk of cramming both a 'this week' time-bound model and an 'ever' structural model into a single combined model?
choices: Either the stable structure gets polluted with fields that go stale within days, or the time-bound facts get wrongly treated as permanent structure
There's no risk -- combining models is always strictly better
The combined model would simply refuse to build
It would make the deploy order faster to compute, with no downside
items.explanation: Mixing timescales in one model means either the durable structural facts get contaminated by fast-changing ones, or the fast-changing ones get frozen in as if permanent -- both are real correctness risks.
items.reference:
📅 'this week': time-bound facts (migrations, flags)
🏗️ 'ever': stable structural dependency edges

Why: The question being asked determines what belongs in the model -- not everything true about the underlying services.

items.prompt: A dependency web has services that each depend on more than one other service (many-to-many relationships). Why would modeling it as a strict tree (one parent per node) be a bad choice, before even writing any code?
choices: A tree structurally cannot represent a node with more than one true dependency, so real edges would have to be dropped to force the data to fit
Trees are always slower to compute with than graphs, regardless of shape
Trees can represent any relationship a graph can, just with different syntax
It would be a fine choice as long as the tree has enough depth
items.explanation: A tree's one-parent-per-node rule is a structural limit, not a style choice -- a service with two real dependencies simply has no way to keep both edges in a tree, so at least one has to be silently dropped.
items.reference:
🌳 tree: one parent per node, by structure
🕸️ graph: any number of edges per node

Why: Choosing a structure that can't represent the real relationships isn't a simplification -- it's a loss of information, worked through concretely in L3.

items.prompt: What real-world signal suggests a dependency web should be modeled as a graph rather than a tree?
choices: At least one thing depends on, or is depended on by, more than one other thing (a many-to-many shape)
The number of services exceeds exactly ten
The team prefers graphs aesthetically over trees
The data is stored in a spreadsheet instead of a database
items.explanation: A tree only fits when every node has at most one parent -- a strictly hierarchical shape. As soon as something needs two or more other things (like `billing` needing both `accounts` and `ledger`), the real shape is a graph, not a tree.
items.reference:
🌳 tree: one parent per node, by structure
🕸️ graph: any number of edges per node

Why: Choosing a structure that can't represent the real relationships isn't a simplification -- it's a loss of information, worked through concretely in L3.

items.prompt: An org chart (each employee has exactly one manager) and a service dependency web (a service can need several others) are both 'relationships between things.' Why does one naturally fit a tree and the other a graph?
choices: The org chart's real-world rule (exactly one manager) matches a tree's one-parent limit; the dependency web's real rule (multiple needs allowed) doesn't, so it needs a graph
Both should always be modeled the same way since both involve relationships
Org charts and dependency webs are actually the same structure with different labels
The choice is arbitrary and has no connection to the real-world rules of either system
items.explanation: The right structure follows from the real-world rule, not from surface similarity. 'Relationships between things' isn't specific enough -- whether multiple parents/dependencies are allowed is what actually decides tree versus graph.
items.reference:
🌳 tree: one parent per node, by structure
🕸️ graph: any number of edges per node

Why: Choosing a structure that can't represent the real relationships isn't a simplification -- it's a loss of information, worked through concretely in L3.

items.prompt: L3's `naiveDeployOrder` runs a single pass over the ten services and returns an empty `result` with all six services skipped. What does this failure look like to someone debugging it, and why is that worse than an error?
choices: It looks like nothing happened -- no error, no indication of which services or why they're stuck, just an empty result
It throws a clear stack trace pointing directly at the cycle
It correctly deploys every service except the ones in the cycle
It crashes the whole process immediately on the first service
items.explanation: The naive pass is a correct implementation of 'check the row order once' -- it just silently produces no progress with no diagnostic, which is much harder to debug than an explicit error naming the cycle.
items.reference:
📋 naive: silent stall, no explanation
🕸️ graph: names the exact cycle

Why: A correct implementation of the wrong approach still fails uninformatively -- the fix is changing the representation, not patching the loop.

items.prompt: L3's Checkpoint asks whether repeating `naiveDeployOrder`'s pass in a loop until no progress is made would fix the cycle problem. What's the actual answer?
choices: It would fix ordering-only failures (a dependency listed later in the file) but the three cycle members would still never become ready, with the same lack of explanation
Yes, repeating the pass enough times always resolves any cycle eventually
No, repeating the pass would cause an infinite loop that crashes the program
It would fix the problem, but only for cycles of exactly three nodes
items.explanation: Repeated passes fix pure ordering issues, but a genuine cycle has no valid order at all -- more passes just take longer to reach the same stuck state, with the same missing explanation.
items.reference:
📋 naive: silent stall, no explanation
🕸️ graph: names the exact cycle

Why: A correct implementation of the wrong approach still fails uninformatively -- the fix is changing the representation, not patching the loop.

items.prompt: In L3's `findCycle`, what does the `"visiting"` state mark, as opposed to `"visited"`?
choices: A node currently on the active DFS path (still being explored above it in the call stack), versus a node whose whole subtree has already finished safely
Whether a node has any dependencies at all
Whether a node's name has already been printed to the console
The total number of edges a node has
items.explanation: "visiting" marks a node still on the current recursive path; "visited" marks one whose exploration is fully done. Hitting a "visiting" node again means the search walked back onto its own path -- a cycle.
items.reference:
🚶 visiting: still on the current path
✅ visited: subtree fully explored, safe

Why: This distinction is exactly what separates 'safe to skip' from 'this is a cycle' during the walk.

items.prompt: Why does `findCycle` need three states (unvisited, visiting, visited) instead of just two (visited, unvisited)?
choices: With only two states, a node whose subtree finished safely would look identical to a node currently on the active path, so a real cycle could go undetected
Three states are needed purely for performance, not correctness
JavaScript's Map data structure requires at least three distinct values
Two states would make the algorithm run faster but less accurately
items.explanation: Without a separate "visiting" state, there's no way to distinguish 'already fully processed' from 'still being processed above me right now' -- exactly the distinction a cycle check depends on.
items.reference:
🚶 visiting: still on the current path
✅ visited: subtree fully explored, safe

Why: This distinction is exactly what separates 'safe to skip' from 'this is a cycle' during the walk.

items.prompt: L3's Checkpoint asks why `topologicalOrder` calls `findCycle` separately instead of treating 'the recursion never terminates' as its own cycle signal. What's the actual reason?
choices: A plain visited-only walk wouldn't fail to terminate -- it would silently mark a cycle member 'visited' partway through and produce a wrong order with no error at all
Because JavaScript recursion always throws a stack overflow on any cyclic graph, which findCycle avoids
Because findCycle runs faster than topologicalOrder for reasons unrelated to correctness
There is no real reason -- the separation is purely stylistic
items.explanation: A two-state walk with a `visited` guard actually does terminate on a cyclic graph -- it just produces a silently wrong order, since it can't tell 'already fully done' from 'still being processed above me.' Separating cycle detection catches that before an order is trusted.
items.reference:
🚶 visiting: still on the current path
✅ visited: subtree fully explored, safe

Why: This distinction is exactly what separates 'safe to skip' from 'this is a cycle' during the walk.

items.prompt: L3's `forceIntoTree` example gives `billing` only one parent even though it genuinely needs both `accounts` and `ledger`. What actually happens to the `ledger` edge?
choices: It's silently deleted -- not deferred or hidden elsewhere, just gone from the model entirely
It's automatically merged into the accounts edge without loss
It's kept as a secondary, lower-priority edge in the same tree
The function throws an error refusing to build an invalid tree
items.explanation: A strict tree only allows one parent per node, so `forceIntoTree` picks the first 'need' and the rest -- including the real `ledger` dependency -- are dropped with no trace.
items.reference:
🌳 tree: forces one parent per node
🕳️ billing's real ledger edge silently vanishes

Why: Forcing a many-to-many relationship into a one-parent structure doesn't simplify the real problem -- it deletes real information to make the data fit.

items.prompt: L3 argues the tree-forced model's wrong deploy order can be worse than the naive checklist's failure. Why?
choices: The checklist at least stalls visibly with no output; the tree model produces a confident, wrong answer with the missing dependency nowhere in sight
The tree model is always slower to compute than the checklist
The checklist and the tree model always produce identical results, so there's no real difference
The tree model requires more lines of code, which is the only downside mentioned
items.explanation: A visible stall at least signals something is wrong. A confidently wrong order from a model that quietly dropped a real dependency edge can ship without anyone noticing until it breaks in production.
items.reference:
🌳 tree: forces one parent per node
🕳️ billing's real ledger edge silently vanishes

Why: Forcing a many-to-many relationship into a one-parent structure doesn't simplify the real problem -- it deletes real information to make the data fit.

items.prompt: According to L3's closing section, what determines whether building a formal model like the dependency graph is actually worth it?
choices: Whether the problem is large or high-stakes enough that manual tracing is guaranteed to eventually miss something, versus small enough to reliably eyeball
Formalizing is always worth it, for every problem, regardless of size
Formalizing is never worth it if the code takes more than 30 minutes to write
Whether the team has a strong preference for graphs over other data structures
items.explanation: The model's build cost is roughly fixed; manual tracing's reliability keeps dropping as the real system grows. The crossover between 'cheap enough to eyeball' and 'guaranteed to eventually miss something' is the actual decision.
items.reference:
⚖️ formalizing has a real, non-zero cost
📈 manual reliability drops as the system grows

Why: Formalizing isn't free, so the decision should track the problem's actual scale and stakes -- not be applied reflexively to everything.

items.prompt: For L3's ten-service example specifically, was building the graph model strictly necessary, or could an experienced engineer plausibly have caught the cycle by hand?
choices: An experienced engineer might well catch it by hand at ten services -- the payoff of formalizing grows as the system gets larger or the stakes get higher, it isn't an all-or-nothing rule
It was strictly necessary -- no human could ever trace ten services by hand
It was unnecessary and provided no benefit over the naive checklist at any scale
The ten-service example proves formal models are only useful above 1,000 services
items.explanation: L1's team did eventually catch a similar cycle by hand -- six months late. Ten services is small enough that manual tracing is plausible but unreliable; the case for formalizing gets stronger, not binary, as scale and stakes increase.
items.reference:
⚖️ formalizing has a real, non-zero cost
📈 manual reliability drops as the system grows

Why: Formalizing isn't free, so the decision should track the problem's actual scale and stakes -- not be applied reflexively to everything.
